title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
gist: Agility Robotics cofounder Jonathan Hurst explains why Digit 5 is a heavy (over 120 kg), forklift-like humanoid rather than the graceful robot he dreamed of. It is built to lift 23-kg bins to 1.75 m for 20 hours a day, run 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, and work safely near people, so safety certification and battery and thermal mass are the main design drivers. He argues that rival humanoids in warehouses fall short on payload, endurance, or safety, and calls Digit 5 Agility's scaling moment, with a factory able to build 10,000+ units a year.

insights.claim: Agility Robotics' Digit 5 humanoid is engineered to lift 23-kg bins onto shelves up to 1.75 m high, matching U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health lifting limits for human workers, and to work 20 hours a day.

insights.so_what: Spec is set by human-labor benchmarks, so the pitch is a direct substitute for a worker on heavy, repetitive warehouse tasks.

insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst

themes.theme: Safety certification as the scaling bottleneck

insights.claim: In Digit 4's commercial deployments, insurance and regulatory demands forced the humanoids to work behind physical barriers, always separated from humans, which severely limited their usefulness.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Without certified human-proximity safety, humanoids are no better than caged industrial arms, and their flexibility advantage is lost.

insights.claim: Agility identified safety as one of the most critical barriers to scaling humanoid robots and spent two years designing Digit 5 to operate safely next to human coworkers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Safety certification, not intelligence, is the near-term gating factor for humanoid adoption and a possible moat for whoever certifies first.

insights.claim: When a person approaches, Digit 5 stops its task, sets down its payload, sits on the floor, and cuts motor power before the person can touch it. Agility believes this is the only verifiable near-term way for humanoids to work near people.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: The first safety approach is conservative, so throughput falls in mixed human-robot zones. Productivity claims should be discounted where people are present.

themes.theme: Bin handling as the wedge market

insights.claim: Agility chose moving warehouse bins as Digit's first job because it is clearly defined, needs two arms to lift large bins high and legs to move in narrow spaces, and varies too much between deployments for single-purpose automation.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Humanoids find their first niche in high-variance tasks that fixed automation cannot address economically, not in general-purpose work.

insights.so_what: Tech-push robotics firms can take years to find product-market fit. Founder-led humanoid startups need patient capital.
